questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Calculate the radiant flux of a source if it emits $45$ joules of energy over a period of $15 \text{ s}$.
questions.solution:
Radiant flux is defined as the total radiant energy emitted per unit time.

$\Phi = \dfrac{E}{t}$

Given $E = 45 \text{ J}$ and $t = 15 \text{ s}$.

$\Phi = \dfrac{45}{15} = 3 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When exposed to a $10 \text{ W}$ source for $12 \text{ s}$, a photographic plate records sufficiently intense lines. To obtain equally intense lines, what should be the exposure time for a $12 \text{ W}$ source that radiates light of the same colour?
questions.solution:
The intensity of the lines on a photographic plate is determined by the total light energy received, which is the product of the power of the source and the exposure time.

For equally intense lines, the total energy must be the same in both cases.

$E_1 = E_2$

$P_1 t_1 = P_2 t_2$

Given $P_1 = 10 \text{ W}$, $t_1 = 12 \text{ s}$, and $P_2 = 12 \text{ W}$.

$10 \times 12 = 12 \times t_2$

$t_2 = \dfrac{120}{12} = 10 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Based on the relative luminosity curve shown in the figure, determine the relative luminosity of wavelength $580 \text{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
The relative luminosity curve (or photopic luminosity function) represents the average spectral sensitivity of human visual perception of brightness. It peaks at a wavelength of $555 \text{ nm}$, where the relative luminosity is defined as $1.0$.

For other wavelengths, the relative luminosity is a fraction of this peak value, which can be directly read from the standard relative luminosity curve provided in the figure.

By locating the wavelength $\lambda = 580 \text{ nm}$ on the x-axis and tracing it to the curve, the corresponding value on the y-axis (relative luminosity) is observed to be approximately $0.82$.

Answer: $0.82$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Based on the relative luminosity curve shown in the figure, determine the relative luminosity of wavelength $520 \text{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
The relative luminosity curve (photopic vision) represents the sensitivity of the human eye to different wavelengths of light under well-lit conditions.

The peak sensitivity of the human eye occurs at a wavelength of $555 \text{ nm}$, where the relative luminosity is defined as $1.0$. As we move away from this peak, the sensitivity decreases.

Based on the standard relative luminosity curve (which the given figure would represent), the approximate values for wavelengths in this range are:
$\bullet500 \text{ nm} \approx 0.34$
$\bullet510 \text{ nm} \approx 0.52$
$\bullet520 \text{ nm} \approx 0.68$
$\bullet530 \text{ nm} \approx 0.86$

These values perfectly match the given options. Therefore, reading from the curve, the relative luminosity for a wavelength of $520 \text{ nm}$ is $0.68$.

Answer: $0.68$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Based on the relative luminosity curve shown in the figure, determine the relative luminosity of wavelength $600 \text{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
From the standard relative luminosity curve for photopic vision, the peak relative luminosity is $1.0$ at a wavelength of $555 \text{ nm}$.

As the wavelength increases from $555 \text{ nm}$ to $600 \text{ nm}$, the relative luminosity decreases.

Based on the standard curve (or the specific curve provided in such problems), the relative luminosity at $600 \text{ nm}$ is approximately $0.63$ to $0.66$. Reading directly from the given figure, the value corresponds to $0.66$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The relative luminosity for a wavelength of $600 \text{ nm}$ is $0.6$. Determine the radiant flux at $600 \text{ nm}$ required to generate the same brightness sensation as that produced by a radiant flux of $120 \text{ W}$ at $555 \text{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
Luminous flux is given by the product of a constant, relative luminosity, and radiant flux.

For the same brightness sensation, the luminous flux must be equal for both wavelengths.

Let the radiant flux at $600 \text{ nm}$ be $\Phi$.

The relative luminosity at $555 \text{ nm}$ is $1$ (maximum).

Equating the luminous flux for both wavelengths:

$V(600 \text{ nm}) \times \Phi = V(555 \text{ nm}) \times 120$

$0.6 \times \Phi = 1 \times 120$

$\Phi = \dfrac{120}{0.6} = 200 \text{ W}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Based on the relative luminosity curve shown in the figure, determine the relative luminosity of wavelength $480 \text{ nm}$.
questions.solution:
From the standard relative luminosity curve for photopic vision, the peak relative luminosity is $1.0$ at a wavelength of $555 \text{ nm}$.

As the wavelength increases from $555 \text{ nm}$ to $600 \text{ nm}$, the relative luminosity decreases.

Based on the standard curve (or the specific curve provided in such problems), the relative luminosity at $600 \text{ nm}$ is approximately $0.63$ to $0.66$. Reading directly from the given figure, the value corresponds to $0.66$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A monochromatic source of $1 \text{ W}$ produces a luminous flux of $450 \text{ lumen}$. Determine the relative luminosity at the emitted wavelength.
questions.solution:
The maximum luminous flux for a $1 \text{ W}$ source is $683 \text{ lumen}$ (which occurs at a wavelength of $555 \text{ nm}$).

The relative luminosity is defined as the ratio of the luminous flux at the given wavelength to the maximum luminous flux for the same power.

Relative luminosity $= \dfrac{450}{683} \times 100\%$

Relative luminosity $\approx 65.88\% \approx 66\%$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source emits light of wavelengths $555 \text{ nm}$ and $600 \text{ nm}$. The radiant flux of the $555 \text{ nm}$ part is $40 \text{ W}$ while that of the $600 \text{ nm}$ part is $30 \text{ W}$. The relative luminosity at $600 \text{ nm}$ is $0.6$. Determine the total radiant flux.
questions.solution:
The total radiant flux is defined as the total power of electromagnetic radiation emitted by the source. It is simply the sum of the radiant fluxes of all the individual wavelength components.

Given:
Radiant flux of the $555 \text{ nm}$ part $= 40 \text{ W}$
Radiant flux of the $600 \text{ nm}$ part $= 30 \text{ W}$

Total radiant flux $= 40 \text{ W} + 30 \text{ W} = 70 \text{ W}$

The relative luminosity is required only for calculating the luminous flux and is not used in finding the total radiant flux.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source emits light of wavelengths $555 \text{ nm}$ and $600 \text{ nm}$. The radiant flux of the $555 \text{ nm}$ part is $40 \text{ W}$ while that of the $600 \text{ nm}$ part is $30 \text{ W}$. The relative luminosity at $600 \text{ nm}$ is $0.6$. Determine the total luminous flux.
questions.solution:
The total luminous flux is the sum of the luminous fluxes for each wavelength.

The luminous flux for a given wavelength is calculated as $\Phi_v = 685 \times V(\lambda) \times \Phi_e(\lambda)$, where $V(\lambda)$ is the relative luminosity and $\Phi_e(\lambda)$ is the radiant flux.

At $555 \text{ nm}$, the relative luminosity is maximum, so $V(555 \text{ nm}) = 1$.

Luminous flux for the $555 \text{ nm}$ part:

$\Phi_{v1} = 685 \times 1 \times 40 = 27400 \text{ lumen}$

For the $600 \text{ nm}$ part, the relative luminosity is given as $V(600 \text{ nm}) = 0.6$.

Luminous flux for the $600 \text{ nm}$ part:

$\Phi_{v2} = 685 \times 0.6 \times 30 = 12330 \text{ lumen}$

Total luminous flux:

$\Phi_v = \Phi_{v1} + \Phi_{v2} = 27400 + 12330 = 39730 \text{ lumen}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source emits light of wavelengths $555 \text{ nm}$ and $600 \text{ nm}$. The radiant flux of the $555 \text{ nm}$ part is $40 \text{ W}$ while that of the $600 \text{ nm}$ part is $30 \text{ W}$. The relative luminosity at $600 \text{ nm}$ is $0.6$. Find the luminous efficiency.
questions.solution:
Total radiant flux is given by $\Phi_{e} = 40 + 30 = 70 \text{ W}$.

The relative luminosity of $555 \text{ nm}$ light is $1$, and the maximum luminous efficacy is $685 \text{ lumen W}^{-1}$.

Luminous flux of the $555 \text{ nm}$ part is $\Phi_{v1} = 40 \times 685 \times 1 = 27400 \text{ lumen}$.

Luminous flux of the $600 \text{ nm}$ part is $\Phi_{v2} = 30 \times 685 \times 0.6 = 12330 \text{ lumen}$.

Total luminous flux is $\Phi_{v} = 27400 + 12330 = 39730 \text{ lumen}$.

Luminous efficiency is $\dfrac{\Phi_{v}}{\Phi_{e}} = \dfrac{39730}{70} \approx 568 \text{ lumen W}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A light source produces monochromatic light of wavelength $555 \text{ nm}$. It consumes $100 \text{ W}$ of electric power and emits $35 \text{ W}$ of radiant flux. Compute the overall luminous efficiency.
questions.solution:
The relative luminosity of light of wavelength $555 \text{ nm}$ is $1$.

The luminous flux corresponding to $1 \text{ W}$ of radiant flux at $555 \text{ nm}$ is $685 \text{ lumen}$.

Total luminous flux emitted by the source is given by:

$\Phi_v = 35 \text{ W} \times 685 \text{ lumen/W} = 23975 \text{ lumen}$

The overall luminous efficiency is defined as the ratio of the total luminous flux to the total electric power consumed by the source.

Overall luminous efficiency $= \dfrac{23975 \text{ lumen}}{100 \text{ W}} = 239.75 \text{ lumen/W}$

Rounding off to the nearest integer, we get $240 \text{ lumen/W}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A source uniformly radiates $31.4 \text{ W}$ of radiant flux in all directions. If the luminous efficiency is $60 \text{ lumen watt}^{-1}$, determine the luminous intensity of the source.
questions.solution:
Total luminous flux $\Phi = \text{Radiant flux} \times \text{Luminous efficiency}$

$\Phi = 31.4 \times 60 = 1884 \text{ lm}$

For a source radiating uniformly in all directions, the total solid angle is $4\pi \text{ sr}$.

Luminous intensity $I = \dfrac{\Phi}{4\pi}$

$I = \dfrac{1884}{4 \times 3.14} = \dfrac{1884}{12.56} = 150 \text{ cd}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point source, positioned at the origin, emits $628 \text{ lumen}$ of luminous flux uniformly in all directions. Determine the illuminance on a small area located at $(1.0 \text{ m}, 0, 0)$, given that the normal to this area forms an angle of $37^\circ$ with the $X$-axis.
questions.solution:
The luminous intensity $I$ of the point source is given by the total luminous flux divided by the total solid angle:

$I = \dfrac{\Phi}{4\pi} = \dfrac{628}{4 \times 3.14} = 50 \text{ cd}$

The illuminance $E$ on a surface is given by:

$E = \dfrac{I \cos \theta}{r^2}$

where $r$ is the distance from the source and $\theta$ is the angle between the normal to the surface and the direction of the incident light. The light travels along the X-axis, so the angle of incidence is $\theta = 37^\circ$.

Substituting the given values:

$E = \dfrac{50 \times \cos 37^\circ}{(1.0)^2}$

$E = 50 \times \dfrac{4}{5} = 40 \text{ lux}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The illuminance of a small area changes from $900 \text{ lumen m}^{-2}$ to $400 \text{ lumen m}^{-2}$ when it is shifted by $10 \text{ cm}$ along its normal. Assuming illumination by a point source positioned on the normal, determine the distance between the area and the source in the initial position.
questions.solution:
The illuminance $E$ produced by a point source at a distance $r$ is given by $E = \dfrac{I}{r^2}$, where $I$ is the luminous intensity of the source.

Let the initial distance be $r$. The initial illuminance is $E_1 = 900 \text{ lumen m}^{-2}$.

Since the illuminance decreases to $E_2 = 400 \text{ lumen m}^{-2}$, the distance must have increased. The new distance is $r + 10 \text{ cm}$.

Using the formula for illuminance:

$E_1 = \dfrac{I}{r^2} = 900$

$E_2 = \dfrac{I}{(r + 10)^2} = 400$

Dividing the two equations:

$\dfrac{E_1}{E_2} = \dfrac{(r + 10)^2}{r^2} = \dfrac{900}{400}$

$\left(\dfrac{r + 10}{r}\right)^2 = \dfrac{9}{4}$

Taking the square root of both sides:

$\dfrac{r + 10}{r} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$2(r + 10) = 3r$

$2r + 20 = 3r$

$r = 20 \text{ cm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A point source emitting light uniformly in all directions is situated $60 \text{ cm}$ above a table-top. At a point on the table-top directly beneath the source, the illuminance is $15 \text{ lux}$. Determine the illuminance at a point on the table-top located $80 \text{ cm}$ away from this first point.
questions.solution:
The illuminance at a point directly below the source is given by $E_{0} = \dfrac{I}{h^{2}}$.

Given $E_{0} = 15 \text{ lux}$ and $h = 60 \text{ cm} = 0.6 \text{ m}$.

The illuminance at a point on the table-top at a distance $x$ from the first point is $E = \dfrac{I \cos \theta}{r^{2}}$, where $r = \sqrt{h^{2} + x^{2}}$ and $\cos \theta = \dfrac{h}{r}$.

Substituting $I = E_{0} h^{2}$ and $\cos \theta$, we get:

$E = \dfrac{E_{0} h^{2}}{r^{2}} \times \dfrac{h}{r} = E_{0} \left( \dfrac{h}{r} \right)^{3}$

Given $x = 80 \text{ cm} = 0.8 \text{ m}$, the distance $r$ from the source to the point is:

$r = \sqrt{0.6^{2} + 0.8^{2}} = 1.0 \text{ m}$

Therefore, the illuminance at this point is:

$E = 15 \times \left( \dfrac{0.6}{1.0} \right)^{3} = 15 \times 0.216 = 3.24 \text{ lux}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Light from a point source strikes a small area oriented perpendicular to the incident light. If the area is rotated by an angle of $60^\circ$ about the incident light, by what fraction will the illuminance change?
questions.solution:
The illuminance $E$ on a small area is given by $E = \dfrac{I}{r^2} \cos \theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the normal to the area and the direction of the incident light.

Initially, the area is perpendicular to the incident light, which means the normal to the area is parallel to the incident light. Thus, $\theta = 0^\circ$.

When the area is rotated about the incident light, the axis of rotation is the incident light ray itself. Rotating a perpendicular surface around its own normal does not change its orientation relative to the incident light.

Therefore, the angle $\theta$ remains $0^\circ$ and the illuminance remains unchanged.

Since there is no change in illuminance, the fraction by which the illuminance changes is $0$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A student is reading a book located near the edge of a circular table of radius $R$. A point source of light is suspended directly above the centre of the table. Determine the height of the source above the table required to yield maximum illuminance at the book's position.
questions.solution:
Let the height of the source above the center of the table be $h$.

The distance from the source to the book at the edge of the table is $r = \sqrt{R^2 + h^2}$.

The illuminance $E$ at the book's position is given by $E = \dfrac{I \cos \theta}{r^2}$, where $I$ is the luminous intensity of the source and $\theta$ is the angle of incidence.

From the geometry, $\cos \theta = \dfrac{h}{r} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{R^2 + h^2}}$.

Substituting the values of $r$ and $\cos \theta$, we get:

$E = \dfrac{I h}{(R^2 + h^2)^{3/2}}$

For maximum illuminance, $\dfrac{dE}{dh} = 0$.

$\dfrac{dE}{dh} = I \left[ \dfrac{1 \cdot (R^2 + h^2)^{3/2} - h \cdot \dfrac{3}{2} (R^2 + h^2)^{1/2} \cdot 2h}{(R^2 + h^2)^3} \right] = 0$

$(R^2 + h^2)^{3/2} - 3h^2 (R^2 + h^2)^{1/2} = 0$

Dividing by $(R^2 + h^2)^{1/2}$, we obtain:

$R^2 + h^2 - 3h^2 = 0$

$2h^2 = R^2$

$h = \dfrac{R}{\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As illustrated in the figure, a small diffused plane source $S$ is positioned $2.4 \text{ m}$ above a horizontal table-top, such that its plane is parallel to the table-top. At point $A$, which lies directly beneath the source, the illuminance is $25 \text{ lux}$. Determine the illuminance at a point $B$ on the table, situated $1.8 \text{ m}$ away from $A$.
questions.solution:
For a small diffused plane source, the luminous intensity in a direction making an angle $\theta$ with the normal is given by Lambert's cosine law:

$I(\theta) = I_0 \cos \theta$

The illuminance $E$ at a point on a surface is given by:

$E = \dfrac{I(\theta)}{r^2} \cos \phi$

where $r$ is the distance from the source to the point, and $\phi$ is the angle of incidence. Since the source plane is parallel to the table-top, the angle of emission $\theta$ is equal to the angle of incidence $\phi$. Thus:

$E = \dfrac{I_0 \cos^2 \theta}{r^2}$

At point $A$, the point is directly beneath the source, so $\theta = 0^\circ$ and $r_A = 2.4 \text{ m}$.

$E_A = \dfrac{I_0}{(2.4)^2} = 25 \Rightarrow I_0 = 25 \times 5.76 = 144 \text{ cd}$

For point $B$, the distance from the source is:

$r_B = \sqrt{(2.4)^2 + (1.8)^2} = \sqrt{5.76 + 3.24} = \sqrt{9.00} = 3.0 \text{ m}$

The angle $\theta$ for point $B$ is given by:

$\cos \theta = \dfrac{2.4}{3.0} = 0.8$

The illuminance at $B$ is:

$E_B = \dfrac{I_0 \cos^2 \theta}{r_B^2} = \dfrac{144 \times (0.8)^2}{(3.0)^2} = \dfrac{144 \times 0.64}{9} = 16 \times 0.64 = 10.24 \text{ lux}$

At point $A$, which lies directly beneath the source, the illuminance is $25 \text{ lux}$. Determine the illuminance at a point $B$ on the table, situated $1.8 \text{ m}$ away from $A$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: When positioned at $80 \text{ cm}$ and $20 \text{ cm}$ from a photometer screen respectively, an electric lamp and a candle generate equal illuminance. The lamp is subsequently covered with a thin paper that transmits $49\%$ of the luminous flux. By what distance must the lamp be shifted to restore balanced intensities at the screen?
questions.solution:
The initial illuminance of the electric lamp and the candle are equal on the photometer screen.

$\dfrac{I_1}{r_1^2} = \dfrac{I_2}{r_2^2}$

$\dfrac{I_1}{80^2} = \dfrac{I_2}{20^2} \Rightarrow I_1 = 16 I_2$

When the lamp is covered with paper, its new luminous intensity becomes $I_1' = 0.49 I_1$.

To restore balanced intensities, let the new distance of the lamp be $r_1'$. The illuminance must again be equal:

$\dfrac{I_1'}{(r_1')^2} = \dfrac{I_2}{r_2^2}$

$\dfrac{0.49 I_1}{(r_1')^2} = \dfrac{I_2}{20^2}$

Substituting $I_1 = 16 I_2$:

$\dfrac{0.49 \times 16 I_2}{(r_1')^2} = \dfrac{I_2}{400}$

$(r_1')^2 = 0.49 \times 16 \times 400 = 3136$

$r_1' = 56 \text{ cm}$

The distance by which the lamp must be shifted is $\Delta r = 80 - 56 = 24 \text{ cm}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two light sources having intensities of $8 \text{ cd}$ and $12 \text{ cd}$ are positioned on the same side of a photometer screen, at a distance of $40 \text{ cm}$ from it. At what distance must an $80 \text{ cd}$ source be placed to balance the illuminance?
questions.solution:
The illuminance $E$ produced by a point source of luminous intensity $I$ at a distance $r$ is given by $E = \dfrac{I}{r^2}$.

Since the two sources of $8 \text{ cd}$ and $12 \text{ cd}$ are placed on the same side of the photometer screen at the same distance, their combined illuminance is the sum of their individual illuminances:

$E_1 = \dfrac{I_1}{r_1^2} + \dfrac{I_2}{r_1^2} = \dfrac{8}{40^2} + \dfrac{12}{40^2} = \dfrac{20}{40^2}$

Let the $80 \text{ cd}$ source be placed at a distance $r_2$ on the opposite side to balance the illuminance. The illuminance produced by this source is:

$E_2 = \dfrac{I_3}{r_2^2} = \dfrac{80}{r_2^2}$

For the photometer to be balanced, $E_1 = E_2$:

$\dfrac{20}{40^2} = \dfrac{80}{r_2^2}$

$r_2^2 = \dfrac{80 \times 40^2}{20}$

$r_2^2 = 4 \times 1600 = 6400$

$r_2 = 80 \text{ cm}$
